rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2.2-3.2 <U+2014> the authors measured electrical parameters (every 10 min), discharge (ultrasonic flowmeters) and pressure head at the Tarazona de La Mancha pumping station during the 2004 season, calibrated a pumping-station efficiency model (Figs 2-8, Table 3) and computed energy/cost savings for alternative pump activation sequences.
rows.notes: The study is a primary case study, but it reports no result on the investment cost of on-demand networks or on guaranteeing supply during peak periods. The network supplied is on-demand, yet the only own results concern pumping-station efficiency calibration, the seasonal discharge distribution, and an energy saving of 14% / cost saving of 16% obtained by operating the two variable-speed pumps sequentially rather than simultaneously (Section 3.2, Conclusions). Investment costs of the network are not analysed; the only investment mentioned is the quick payback of the monitoring instruments. Mention of optimising investment plus energy costs refers to other studies (Moradi-Jalal et al., Pulido-Calvo et al., Planells et al.), not to the study's own findings. Hence no own evidence on the claim.

notes: Full text appears complete (pages 479-486). Study is an energy-efficiency case study of one pumping station in Spain; it is cited here for a claim about investment costs of on-demand networks that it does not itself address.
